📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.
  • This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality.
  • According to recent reports, ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

According to recent reports, ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl.

It has been revealed that iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola mentioned. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”.

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”.

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE.

Industry observers note that iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola remarked of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

According to recent reports, “We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he noted, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

In a recent development, dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”.

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

In a recent development, liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

According to recent reports, they have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

Recent findings suggest that the bananas are disappearing now winter is coming, the fire and fury waning with each passing week. In legal limbo, Manchester City’s supporters need something – anything – to stand behind but increasingly their team refuse to provide that solace.

Recent findings suggest that city were booed off at the end as Enzo Maresca ducked down the tunnel. Some of that could have been directed at referee Thomas Bramall, after Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal, but certainly a significant number were jeering what they’d just seen. That simply does not happen at the Etihad Stadium, even during the torrid run of two years ago.

According to recent reports, but they are witnessing a squad who radiate uncertainty. Who take three touches when two will do; who always receive possession squarely facing their own goal; who do not create passing lines for their mates. And crucially, who are forever momentarily confused as to who exactly is picking up which runner and those split seconds make all the difference in this division.

In a recent development, there is just this strange state of unease around how they want to approach games at the moment, something that adversity can provoke and something that Maresca is adamant he can correct. A coach of his calibre should do given the time and freedom.

Yet when he spent the two-week international break studying clips and fashioning ways of improving, he cannot have envisaged a scenario whereby home fans were so incredulous at a lack of energy that they were roused to their feet when Haaland deigned to close down Bernd Leno and force an error.

Man City put in an underwhelming performance as they were held to a 1-1 draw by Fulham.

Enzo Maresca's side are radiating uncertainty and look worryingly vulnerable at the back.

Rodrigo Muniz made City pay as he put an impressive Fulham 1-0 ahead after 16 minutes.

Fulham popped it about nicely and at will. Found pockets to hurt their illustrious hosts, who were again asking a centre half – in this case Marc Guehi – to charge into midfield. City did have more balance than at Nottingham Forest for including Ayyoub Bouaddi for Enzo Fernandez, yet Alvaro Arbeloa still aggressively pressed them in that area to some success.

‘I told the players that we will have the chance to beat them if we play with courage,’ remarked Arbeloa, who was indebted to the towering performance of defender David Affengruber.

In a recent development, arsenal will have watched this grinning and could easily be racking up an unassailable lead once these teams meet in north London next Sunday. Unassailable with all the usual caveats about the appeal and what this season may or may not eventually mean.

City did create enough statistically but as with other games of late, that did not tell the whole story.

Calvin Bassey pirouetted through midfield, the heavily derided Gianluigi Donnarumma thwarting a number of strong Fulham chances, and City appeared somewhat lost and out of ideas.

Elliot Anderson equalised with a superb volley but City failed to create much after that.

Maresca expressed his concern at City's lack of clean sheets after they struggled again.

That is a worrying departure from recent defeats, where they attacked with the same abandon as that early season flourish when they might as well have hosted games at Madison Square Gardens and played with an orange ball.

MAN CITY (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 7; Khusanov 6, Dias 6, Guehi 5, O’Reilly 5 (Gvardiol 78); Anderson 7, Bouaddi 7 (Fernandez 85); Ndiaye 6 (Allan 78), Foden 7 (Cherki 70), Doku 5; Haaland 5.

FULHAM (4-2-3-1): Leno 6; Tete 6, Affengruber 8, Bassey 7, Sessegnon 7 (Palacios 83); Berge 6, Charles 7; Bobb 7 (Garcia 78), King 6 (Larsson 70, 6), Iwobi 7 (Robinson 70, 6); Muniz 7 (Cairney 83).

Met with a Fulham who had not conceded more than once in the league since the start of September, City failed to create a meaningful opportunity in the last 25 minutes of a match they were desperate to win and should have been in the ascendancy of after Elliot Anderson’s volleyed equaliser after half time.

Maresca, though, is more concerned with a lack of clean sheets. It’s now none of those in nine games in all competitions for the first time in seven years, with Rodrigo Muniz opening the scoring on 16 minutes. A throw inside Fulham’s own third prompted Guehi to jump and lose his duel, City turned around and Oscar Bobb laid on for Muniz.

‘We’re conceding too many goals,’ Maresca said. ‘We need to avoid it. You need to win games 1-0. You need clean sheets. We’re not able to do it. But I can see many positive aspects. We started four months ago and not four years ago.

‘We’ve conceded almost 80 per cent of our goals at the start of the first half and second half. It’s something we need to improve. It’s a throw in at the corner flag and nobody is expecting they can create something.’.

Maresca was also insistent that Haaland ought to have been awarded an equaliser before the break when poking in on the goal line, yet Bramall adjudged that Leno had the ball under control on field, with VAR not overruling.

Some hard luck, some profligacy with Haaland squandering a couple of big chances, but the day was summed up when in stoppage time, Jeremy Doku was penalised for a foul throw.

Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
  • Industry observers note that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.
  • Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

Industry observers note that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care. In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

Industry observers note that the 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

In a recent development, half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

According to recent reports, exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a fresh cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that for people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Recent findings suggest that even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

It has been revealed that earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

It has been revealed that CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

Industry observers note that "I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Recent findings suggest that nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he mentioned.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she mentioned.

Sources indicate that nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he stated.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together.".

According to recent reports, campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she stated.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

Recent findings suggest that according to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and tech giant. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

The 32-year-old is unhappy with both the proposed salary and the length of the deal, and the standoff lands with his current contract set to expire in June 2027.

The calendar adds pressure. In 50 days, Fernandes can open talks with foreign clubs, and Galatasaray have already been linked. United hold a 12-month extension option that stops him leaving for free, but triggering it only postpones the argument and keeps an unhappy captain in the dressing room.

Carrick has since been sacked with United 18th in the Premier League, inside the relegation zone, so Mauricio Pochettino inherits the standoff alongside a team in trouble.

His strengths are obvious. He set a Premier League record with 21 assists last season, delivers set pieces better than anyone at the club and opened this campaign with a hat-trick against Ipswich. His weaknesses are just as clear. At 32, the Portuguese international gives little protection when United lose the ball, and his shot selection can be wasteful.

Recent findings suggest that pochettino’s best sides pressed hard and ran through a creative number ten with two athletic midfielders behind him. Fernandes suits the creative role, but only if those two midfielders cover his space.

Sources indicate that united should keep him, but on shorter terms than he wants. Nobody else in the squad creates chances at his rate, and a team sitting in the bottom three cannot replace that in January. A long, expensive deal for a player entering his mid-thirties would create a wage problem just as Pochettino tries to rebuild the midfield around younger runners.

In a recent development, the sensible offer is a short contract with a raise tied to appearances and Champions League qualification. That respects his standing without committing United beyond the point where his legs start to fail.

If Fernandes still refuses, the board should trigger the extension and sell next summer. A sale with a year left on his deal will still bring a meaningful fee, whereas losing him for nothing in 2027 would waste the one asset United can sell on their own terms.

Recent findings suggest that the hosts are in strong form. This was their second 4-0 win in a row, after beating Dolomiti Bellunesi by the same score. Lecco have now scored 15 goals in four games.

#60344. Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 90m • 📚 Deep Dive (18005 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 90 min read (18005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~90 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1.
  • It has been revealed that solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5.
  • It has been revealed that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope2,3. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours.

It has been revealed that solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5. Within the TME, both stromal and immune cells have emerged as key modulators of tumour growth, invasion and metastasis1,6,7,8,9,10. However, different studies (often in single-organ contexts) have shown conflicting roles for these cells in promoting versus suppressing tumour growth11,12,13,14. The heterogeneity of the TME, both within individual tumours and across tumour types, poses a substantial challenge to understanding the functional diversity of tumour-associated stromal and immune cells3,15,16.

It has been revealed that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21. However, these findings stem largely from isolated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies22,23,24, and subsequent pan-cancer efforts have remained limited in size and scope3,25,26,27,28. To our knowledge, the largest cancer-associated fibroblast atlas to date integrates data from 1,116 samples across 10 tumour types29; the largest tumour endothelial cell atlas includes 575 samples across 19 tumour types30; and no specific tumour mural or nerve atlases have been generated. Pan-cancer immune cell atlases have been larger28, especially those focused on individual immune cell lineages31,32,33; however, these typically have not examined immune cell interactions within the broader TME.

It has been revealed that here we integrated single-cell transcriptomic data from 3,381 human and mouse samples across 42 cancer types and 258 datasets to create a definitive TME transcriptional atlas. By mapping this massive cellular landscape, we resolved the stromal and immune ecosystem of solid tumours. Furthermore, by linking enriched subpopulations to poor clinical outcomes, we identified opportunities for future TME-targeted cancer therapies. Key computational predictions are subsequently validated through in vitro and in vivo experiments. Finally, we have consolidated this work into an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and R software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for groups investigating the TME.

It has been revealed that to systematically analyse single-cell transcriptomic data, we evaluated every scRNA-seq cancer study published in the public domain between January 2014 and July 2025. Separate queries were evaluated independently for human and mouse datasets within the foundational public repositories for single-cell transcriptomics: the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. We screened a total of 3,975 published datasets (Fig. 1a). Studies specific to either blood or central nervous system cancers were excluded from our analysis, as were those failing to meet specific architectural requirements (Methods; see Fig. 1a,b). Our comprehensive screen identified 190 human and 68 mouse datasets (Supplementary Table 1), collectively comprising more than 15.4 million cells. Collectively, these datasets formed the final analytical cohort, comprising 3,381 individual scRNA-seq samples across 42 unique cancer types (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).

a, Systematic workflow detailing the scRNA-seq dataset curation process. The initial screen examined 3,975 datasets, of which 190 human and 68 mouse scRNA-seq remained after filtering. The combined 258 datasets comprised 3,381 samples and more than 15 million cells. Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). CNS, central nervous system. b, Illustration of all cancer types from human (top) and mouse (bottom) included in this study. HNSCC, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; MPNST, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; NSCLC, non-small-cell lung cancer; SCLC, small-cell lung cancer. Illustration created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/p0byno1 (2026).

Industry observers note that to process the more than 12.8 million human cells from 2,855 samples and 190 datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 1), nearly an order of magnitude greater than many recent seminal studies3,25,26,27,28,31,32,33,34, we used sketch-based sampling and memory read optimization (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). We applied three independent approaches for data integration to reduce batch effects: Harmony, scVI and FastMNN (Extended Data Figs. 1e and 2a). We then projected each integrated result onto the full dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Supervised annotation using four methods—canonical marker genes, estimated copy number variation (inferCNV), SingleR and scATOMIC (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2)—delineated the presence of seven main cell types across nearly all human cancers (Fig. 2a–c, Extended Data Fig. 1e,f and Supplementary Table 4). These encompass principal stromal (fibroblast, endothelial, mural and nerve) and immune (myeloid and lymphoid) lineages, alongside epithelial cells, which were excluded from subsequent characterization to focus on the two core TME compartments. Comparing the three integration approaches (Supplementary Table 5), Harmony demonstrated the most robust integration and was selected for all subsequent evaluations. The three integration approaches also frequently yielded discordant cell-type assignments for individual cells (Extended Data Fig. 2d–f), highlighting the stochasticity and misclassification risks inherent to relying on any single method35,36. To mitigate this, we provisionally pooled all cells assigned to a specific TME lineage by any of the three algorithms (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Misassigned cells within these overlapping pools were subsequently removed through recursive downstream filtering (Extended Data Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 3a–e), generating final, high-fidelity atlases for the six principal TME cell types (Fig. 2d–i and Extended Data Fig. 1i,j).

a, UMAP embeddings of 12,855,771 cells from 190 human studies integrated using Harmony, with consensus seven cell-type annotations (outlined and labelled within the panel) derived through multiple annotation approaches (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3). Individual cells are labelled according to downstream final cell annotations in panels d–i. cDC, conventional dendritic cell; DC, dendritic cell; End, endothelial; Fib, fibroblast; Lym, lymphoid; Mac, macrophage; mem, memory; Mono, monocyte; mregDC, mature dendritic cell enriched in immunoregulatory molecules; Mur, mural; myel, myelinating; Myl, myeloid; Neut, neutrophil; NK, natural killer; SMC, smooth muscle cell; TFH, follicular helper T; Treg, regulatory T. b, Total number of human samples included for each type of cancer. c, Distribution of cell types for each cancer, after selecting for only unsorted samples. Abbreviations of cancer names are listed in Supplementary Table 2. d, UMAP embedding of CAFs, manually clustered into four parent populations (outlined and labelled within the UMAP) from a total of seven transcriptionally distinct subpopulations, the latter of which are coloured separately (top left). A dot plot displaying relative gene expression for characteristic markers of the seven transcriptionally distinct CAF subpopulations shown in the left panel (top right). Distributions of CAF subpopulations among tumour samples for different cancer types are also shown (bottom; n = 328,877 cells). e–i, UMAPs (top left), dot plots (top right) and distributions among tumour samples for different cancer types (bottom) for endothelial (e; n = 234,948 cells), mural (f; n = 162,178 cells), nerve (g; n = 7,655 cells), lymphoid (h; n = 1,580,785 cells) and myeloid (i; n = 805,111 cells) cells. Between 3 and 12 subpopulations are identified for each cell type, and one population-defining gene per subpopulation is displayed in the dot plot for each cell type (full list in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7).

We next characterized cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), the predominant stromal population in the TME37. Following our recursive isolation strategy (Extended Data Fig. 1h), we delineated four transcriptionally distinct CAF meta-clusters (Fig. 2d) expressing canonical markers (PDGFRA, LUM and DCN) and lacking non-fibroblast markers (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, we identified (1) antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs; class II HLA+), (2) immunomodulatory/inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs; cytokine+), (3) myofibroblastic/mechanoresponsive CAFs (mCAFs; extracellular matrix (ECM)+, mechanotransduction+), and (4) steady-state CAFs (ssCAFs; progenitor-like markers+; Fig. 2d), broadly consistent with observations from our previous work38 and that of others25,39,40,41. High-resolution sub-clustering (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Table 6 and 7 and Supplementary Fig. 4) further stratified these into seven subpopulations: two iCAF (CXCL8+ or ISG15+), two mCAF (LRRC15+ or COL4A1+), two ssCAF (PI16+ or CXCL14+) and one apCAF. All seven subpopulations were conserved across nearly all evaluated tumour types and tissues (Fig. 2d, bottom). Of note, apCAFs were nearly universally present, whereas previous studies had found them only in rare tumour subsets6. Furthermore, the human apCAFs that we identified did not express mesothelial markers such as MSLN, which are characteristic of mouse apCAFs42 (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

Comparing relative abundances between tumour and non-malignant tissues (Fig. 3a), both mCAF populations were significantly enriched in tumours (3.5-fold for LRRC15+; 2.7-fold for COL4A1+; Supplementary Table 8), reflecting cancer-induced desmoplasia37,43. Similarly, iCAFs and apCAFs were enriched in tumour samples (6.3-fold for ISG15+ iCAFs, 1.3-fold for CXCL8+ iCAFs and 2.0-fold for apCAFs), consistent with their roles in inducing immune evasion42 or secreting inflammatory cytokines41. Analysing abundance across tumour stage and patient treatment response, we found ISG15+ iCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs and COL4A1+ mCAFs significantly enriched in late-stage (III–IV) versus early-stage (I–II) tumours (1.9-fold, 1.3-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3b). Treatment responsiveness did not significantly correlate with any CAF subpopulation (Fig. 3c). Overall, ISG15+ iCAFs were the most consistently enriched fibroblast subset defining both the malignant state and advanced disease (Fig. 3a–c, blue box).

Focusing on the iCAF compartment, our atlas revealed two distinct and conserved transcriptional states: ISG15+ iCAFs exhibiting canonical interferon-γ (IFNγ) stimulation (for example, CXCL10)44, and CXCL8+ iCAFs expressing pro-inflammatory cytokines (for example, CXCL1)41. Crucially, these iCAF subpopulations provide additional granularity compared with previously reported CXCL12+ iCAFs39. Recent consensus frameworks have identified CXCL12 to be among the steady-state fibroblast hallmark genes rather than specific to a malignancy-induced inflammatory CAF state25. In line with this, our CXCL14+ ssCAFs co-expressed high levels of CXCL12 while maintaining a homeostatic signature. Abundance analyses revealed divergent ssCAF dynamics: conventional PI16+ ssCAFs (which also strongly express CXCL12) were heavily enriched in non-malignant tissue (2.8-fold), potentially representing a progenitor pool, whereas the CXCL14+ pool remained proportionally stable across benign and malignant tissues (1.0-fold), typifying embedded parenchymal fibroblasts. We therefore propose that traditional ‘CXCL12+ iCAFs’ are more accurately classified as tissue-resident CXCL14+ ssCAFs.

To elucidate the regulatory networks driving these distinct states, we examined transcription factor activity using SCENIC. The apCAF population exhibited elevated inferred activity of RUNX3 and IKZF1, regulators of MHC class II expression45, suggesting a mechanism for direct T cell interaction and immunotherapy resistance (Extended Data Fig. 5a). The ISG15+ iCAFs highlighted predicted activation of ETV7 and IRF2, implicating suppressive cytokine signalling in tumour progression46 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Both mCAF populations were enriched for CREB3L1 and NKX3-2, linked to ECM overexpression and stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Conversely, ssCAF populations exhibited higher predicted activity of CEBPA and FOXO3, which regulate lineage and redox homeostasis, respectively, consistent with the homeostatic properties ascribed to this population26 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Overall, these regulatory profiles broadly align with the putative functional roles attributed to each CAF subpopulation.

To evaluate whether specific populations could be distinguished by differences in metabolic programs, we applied scMetabolism to analyse our scRNA-seq dataset. Of note, we observed that LRRC15+ mCAFs were enriched for genes associated with elevated oxidative phosphorylation, in contrast to the traditional glycolytic programs of ISG15+ iCAFs (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f and Supplementary Fig. 5a–c). These profiles align with the distinct energy demands of each cell type: iCAFs expressed genes linked with rapid glycolytic ATP generation that would permit overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, whereas mCAFs were predicted to utilize the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation, enabling them to sustain intense ECM production and remodelling driving the desmoplastic response to neoplasia47. ssCAFs exhibited globally lower expression of metabolic pathway genes, reinforcing their relatively quiescent state.

According to recent reports, to determine whether these distinct functional and metabolic states ultimately impact patient survival, we paired bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) using CIBERSORTx deconvolution (Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 6a,b). Patients whose tumours were estimated to have higher abundances of apCAFs, iCAFs or mCAFs exhibited worse overall survival across most cancer types, consistent with previous observations48. By contrast, we observed a positive (but not statistically significant; 1.3-fold, P = 0.27) relationship between CXCL14+ ssCAF proportion and patient survival. Together, these results suggest that fibroblast differentiation and lineage progression may be associated with worse outcomes in solid-organ tumours, reflecting a pro-tumorigenic role for apCAFs, iCAFs and mCAFs.

According to recent reports, beyond fibroblasts, we examined tumour endothelial, mural and nerve cells, which drive angiogenesis, cytokine signalling and metastatic spread1,7,8,49. In silico isolation of endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–j) identified five pan-cancer subpopulations (Fig. 2e): GJA5+ arterial, CA4+ capillary, PROX1+ lymphatic, ESM1+ tip and ACKR1+ venous. All expressed canonical markers (PECAM1, VWF and CDH5) and lacked non-endothelial signatures (Extended Data Fig. 4b, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7). Of note, angiogenic ESM1+ tip cells50 were the sole endothelial subpopulation significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (1.7-fold; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), reflecting dysfunctional tumour neovascularization51. These tip cells, co-expressing FLT1 (VEGFR1) and KDR (VEGFR2), were significantly elevated in treatment non-responsive tumours (1.9-fold; Fig. 3c). Furthermore, they correlated with elevated metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 5d) and worse overall survival across most TCGA cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 6b). These data reinforce the pro-tumorigenic role of tip cells7,52,53, which may continuously support growth by rapidly initiating marginal angiogenesis, highlighting them as candidate targets for multi-drug therapy.

Subclustering of pan-cancer mural cells delineated six distinct subpopulations (Fig. 2f): CCL2+, CD248+ and ISG15+ pericytes; RERGL+ and WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells; and DES+ visceral smooth muscle cells. All expressed canonical markers (RGS5, PDGFRB and CSPG4) and lacked non-mural signatures (Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 8). ISG15+ and CD248+ pericytes, alongside WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells, were significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (4.5-fold, 1.8-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), with ISG15+ pericytes also exhibiting elevated overall metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Clinically, CD248+ pericytes correlated with poor treatment response (1.8-fold; Fig. 3c). Mechanistically, both tumour-enriched pericyte populations expressed ECM genes (COL1A1, COL3A1 and COL4A1), supporting a role in tumour desmoplasia (Supplementary Fig. 5e,f). Of note, PIEZO2, which encodes a mechanotransduction channel, was detected in a small subset of CD248+ pericytes and was not detected in other mural populations (Supplementary Fig. 8). Detection was sparse and expression levels were low, indicating selective rather than robust population-specific expression. Given the established role of PIEZO2 in cellular mechanosensation54, we hypothesize that this fraction of pro-fibrotic pericytes may be activated by the stiffened TME to further upregulate ECM production, a possibility that merits further investigation.

Finally, we analysed tumour-associated nerve cells, filtering out neural crest cancers to avoid transcriptional overlap with nerve-based tumours49. Our analysis revealed three distinct subpopulations and their canonical markers: MLANA+ melanocytes, MPZ+ myelinating Schwann cells and NGFR+ non-myelinating Schwann cells (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Subpopulation proportions varied markedly across tumour types (Fig. 2g, bottom). Because this heterogeneity probably reflects both tissue-specific neural architecture and the general rarity of nerve cells in standard biopsies, these populations were omitted from subsequent downstream analyses.

Comprising over 2.4 million cells, immune cells constituted the largest TME compartment in our atlas. In silico isolation broadly segregated these into lymphoid and myeloid lineages. Focusing first on lymphoid cells—primary mediators of antitumour immunity55—we identified 11 subpopulations: CD4+ (3) and CD8+ (3) T cells, natural killer cells (1), B cells (3) and plasma cells (1; Fig. 2h, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 10). Nearly all T cell populations were significantly enriched in tumours (Fig. 3a). This was driven primarily by CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (2.4-fold) and CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive exhausted T (TEX) cells (1.5-fold). Of note, this GZMB+ population was also significantly enriched in early-stage disease (Fig. 3b), reflecting an initial wave of localized antitumour immunity undergoing rapid, chronic antigen-driven dysfunction56. In addition, FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (1.8-fold) and CXCL13+ follicular helper T cells (1.6-fold) were both enriched in tumours. By contrast, B cell and plasma populations were comparatively depleted within the tumour but enriched in non-malignant tissue, probably reflecting peritumoural accumulation and immune exclusion from the tumour core57.

According to recent reports, examining tumour myeloid cells, we identified dendritic cells (three populations), monocytes (two populations), macrophages (four populations), mast cells, neutrophils and osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 11). Most spanned all tumour types, except the tissue-specific osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, bottom). Three macrophage subtypes and LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells were significantly tumour enriched (Fig. 3a), with SPP1+ and MARCO+ subpopulations further enriched in late-stage disease (Fig. 3b). SPP1+ macrophages (GPNMB+ and APOC1+) are known drivers of desmoplasia and poor clinical outcomes32, whereas late-stage MARCO+ enrichment suggests a specialized role in immunosuppression and hindered phagocytosis. Conversely, C1QC+ macrophages maintain a homeostatic, complement-rich signature (C1QA–C and FOLR2) linked to T cell infiltration and a non-exhausted TME58. LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells (IDO1+ and CCR7+) represent a critical regulatory checkpoint, limiting cytotoxic T cell activity to facilitate late-stage immune evasion59. Finally, shared ISG15+ ‘IFN-primed’ clusters across both macrophages and T cells suggest a common axis of chronic inflammation driving terminal exhaustion via sustained type I IFN signalling31,32.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate alignment with broader transcriptional consensus models, we performed quantitative cell-level comparisons against four pan-cancer reference atlases using pairwise expression mapping via our scTME software package60 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Most of our subpopulations exhibited strong, reciprocal alignment with comparable cell types across datasets (for example, PI16+ ssCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs, ESM1+ tip cells, C1QC+/SPP1+ macrophages and FOXP3+ regulatory T cells). These comparisons also differentiated several of our newly characterized and finely partitioned subpopulations. The IFN-primed (ISG15+) axis mapped robustly to analogous IFN-activated states across lineages (Extended Data Fig. 6b). In addition, our newly identified ISG15+ pericytes mapped to parent pericytes (Extended Data Fig. 6a) but diverged from CD248+ pericytes in broader TME atlases by lacking myofibroblast overlap, reinforcing their distinct state (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Furthermore, CXCL14+ fibroblasts mapped predominantly to non-inflammatory populations—unlike the CXCL8+ and ISG15+ iCAF subpopulations—supporting their separation from canonical iCAFs. Overall, although our TME atlas is broadly congruent with established datasets, our fibroblast and mural subpopulations reflect a uniquely refined, data-driven partitioning with functional relevance.

Our meta-analysis identified apCAFs across nearly all evaluated tumour types (Fig. 2d, bottom), far exceeding the limited number of cancers in which they have been validated in vivo6. Therefore, we performed immunohistochemistry to confirm their presence in previously uncharacterized tumour types. Co-staining for the membranous fibroblast marker PDGFRα and the antigen-presenting marker HLA-DR confirmed apCAF presence in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) controls61, as well as in previously non-validated colorectal cancer (CRC) and papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) tissues, as predicted by our atlas (Fig. 3d). To exclude possible immune cell misclassification, we analysed multiplexed spatial proteomic (CODEX) data from human PDAC62. Spindle-like HLA-DR+ cells localized to highly fibrotic (COL1A1+/αSMA+) regions, lacked immune or epithelial markers (Fig. 3g,h), and occupied distinct ECM architectures associated with poor patient outcomes (Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Fig. 12a–f). We further orthogonally validated apCAF presence using public Xenium spatial transcriptomic datasets63,64 (Supplementary Fig. 13a–c). scRNA-seq revealed only a modest correlation between apCAF and T cell abundances in tumour samples (Supplementary Fig. 14a), suggesting that apCAF expansion occurs regional to but independent of direct T cell support. By contrast, ISG15+ iCAFs strongly correlated with CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (Supplementary Fig. 14b), supporting our hypothesis that this CAF population interacts with T cells to drive exhaustion and promote immune evasion.

In a recent development, to infer interaction networks, we paired CellChat receptor–ligand predictions with orthogonal NicheNet modelling of downstream transcriptional targets. Because multiple lineages harboured ISG15+ clusters, we first evaluated the IFNγ network. CellChat predicted robust signalling from CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive TEX cells to ISG15+ iCAFs (Fig. 4a), which was corroborated by NicheNet (Fig. 4b). These aligned predictions support the hypothesis that ISG15+ iCAFs act as direct responders to chronic, T cell-derived IFNγ within the TME. Applying this approach to explore drivers of dysfunctional neovascularization, CellChat predicted that ESM1+ endothelial tip cells receive disproportionately high VEGF signalling from tumour-associated macrophages and monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7a). NicheNet further corroborated this relationship (Extended Data Fig. 7b), successfully recapitulating this established myeloid-driven angiogenic axis using data solely from our atlas65. Conversely, NicheNet did not directly substantiate several other CellChat-predicted receptor–ligand pairings as transcriptional drivers, suggesting that these specific interactions may operate via indirect or non-transcriptional mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d and Supplementary Fig. 15a–d).
